source.title: Geometric Regularization from Overparameterization explains Double Descent and other findings

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent and proposes a geometric explanation, but does not measure test error across model sizes, epochs, or training-set sizes, or test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports exploratory measurements of loss-value histograms from randomly initialized toy networks, but these are not measurements of double-descent test error or of the peak locations named in the versions. Its model-capacity, epoch-wise, and data-fidelity curves are described as prior findings or proposed hypotheses. The Higgs noise-augmentation benchmark is attributed to earlier work and is not counted as a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The paper offers a speculative geometric conjecture for double descent. Its own experiments are histograms of loss values from randomly initialized, untrained small networks on 3 Titanic features. None of them measures test error against model size, epochs or sample count. The double-descent curves in Figs 2, 3 and 5 are cited or hypothesized, not measured. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conjecture that volume contraction of weight-set distributions with overparameterization gives implicit 'geometric regularization'. They hold that double descent arises when the intrinsic dimension of available update steps shrinks across a hypersphere-like volume peak. They suggest interpolation thresholds depend on data representation fidelity. They call the threshold discussion speculative and the histograms tangential.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a geometric explanation and explores initialized loss-distribution histograms; it does not reproduce the original double-descent test-error sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported histogram patterns vary with width, depth, activation, initialization scale and distribution, and the number of training samples included in the loss.

fits_no_version.finding: For untrained randomly initialized small networks, the shape of sampled BCE loss histograms shifts with width, depth, activation, initialization scale and distribution, and with the number of samples averaged into the loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The distribution of loss values over randomly initialized weights depends on architecture and initialization (exploratory; not a double-descent measure).

record.problems: The paper does not test double-descent test-error curves. Its own empirical work is exploratory, based on randomly initialized small networks and histogram sampling; the authors note that some low-loss tails were invisible at their sampling rate and that the histograms do not reveal volume directly. Several statements about double descent are conjectures or cited findings.
record.rows_left_out: The Higgs noise-augmentation AUC table in Appendix C is described as benchmarking detailed in Teague (2022), so it is treated as an earlier-work result rather than this study's own result. Other figure examples and histogram variations are not separately extracted where the text gives no additional distinct outcome beyond the reported conditions.

untested.parts: No test-error sweep over model size; Fig 2 is reproduced from Belkin et al.
Epoch-wise double descent is explained by conjecture only, with no training curves.
The 'data fidelity double descent' (Fig 5) is hypothesized, not measured.
Results on other model classes are cited only.
The paper argues the interpolation threshold depends on data fidelity and intrinsic dimension, but measures nothing.
Regularization dampening the peak and noise shifting the threshold are cited (Belkin; Dhifallah & Lu), not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to none: they are untrained loss-histogram explorations. The Higgs AUC table comes from Teague (2022) and concerns noise augmentation versus data scale, not double descent; excluding it is correct. Several of the paper's figures (2, 3, 4) are reproduced from cited works.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep across model sizes or interpolation threshold.
No test-error measurement over training epochs.
No experiment varying training-sample count and measuring test error near an interpolation threshold.
No test of double descent across model classes.
No measurement testing whether one effective-complexity measure predicts double-descent peak locations.
No test of noise, regularization, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization on double descent.
No test of whether re-counting complexity turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.value: With more depth, density shifted toward the central mode, in the direction opposite to increasing width.
rows.note: The text reports the direction of the histogram change; it does not report test error.

rows.subject: small network (architecture not otherwise stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared sampled loss-value histograms as the number of training samples included in the loss increased.
rows.measure: Representation of the low-loss left tail in the histogram
rows.value: Averaging loss over multiple samples greatly diminished the left tail; for 50 samples it was not visible at the applied sampling rate.
rows.locator: Appendix D, Figure 8; Appendix I, Figures 18–20
rows.note: The authors state that the tail may still exist below their sampling visibility; this is not a test-error result.

rows.subject: small network (architecture not otherwise stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared sampled loss-value histograms for ReLU and tanh activations.
rows.measure: Histogram modes and variation with architecture
rows.value: ReLU histograms showed sharp peaks; in many small-width cases a secondary mode appeared, and ReLU shifted more noticeably with architecture variation.
rows.note: The reported measure is the initialized loss histogram, not model generalization or double descent.

rows.measure: Histogram modes and variation with architecture
rows.value: Tanh histograms were generally smoother and more stable across architecture variations, with one visible mode; a slight zero-mode shift appeared in some large-width cases.
rows.note: The reported measure is the initialized loss histogram, not model generalization or double descent.
